izzyondroid:eu.micer.clipboardservice.summary: service that accepts a string and saves it to clipboard
izzyondroid:eu.micer.clipboardservice.description:
clipboard-service is a simple Android service that accepts the string and saves it to clipboard. It can be used to save string from computer to clipboard in Android device.
 Usage 
 Run these commands from computer's command-line terminal. Device needs to be connected via ADB .
 # Start service and pass a string value to be saved in device's clipboard:
adb shell am startservice -a eu.micer.ClipboardService -e text "SampleText"
# Invoke paste action:
adb shell input keyevent 279 
 Not working? 
 It can happen that you get this error:
 ~ adb shell am startservice -a eu.micer.ClipboardService -e text "SampleText"
Starting service: Intent { act=eu.micer.ClipboardService (has extras) }
Error: app is in background uid null 
 You just need to start the app via command:
 adb shell am start -n eu.micer.clipboardservice/eu.micer.clipboardservice.EmptyActivity 
 or find the ClipboardService in the app list and start it manually.

fdroid:com.dailybeat.app.description:
DailyBeat helps you remember your day with a journal stored on your Android phone. Capture journeys when you choose, add notes, review visits and turn your records into an editable daily draft. No account or cloud AI is required.
 Personal, Field work and Police writing templates.
 Optional background journey capture using Android location APIs, without Google Play Services.
 Search notes, diaries and recorded places; name or hide stops and define private zones.
 Create local drafts, review changes and preview PDF or weekly ZIP exports before sharing.
 View routes with MapLibre and OpenStreetMap data. Download a separate Tamil Nadu street map for offline viewing, including local fonts and labels.
 Pause and resume verified map downloads; use Wi-Fi by default and explicitly allow mobile data when needed.
 Choose local retention, delete records, and use light or dark mode.
 Online maps are enabled by default. Map providers can see your IP address and requested areas. Turn off Allow online maps under Settings, Capture & Places to use downloaded maps or a route-only preview. Manual Tamil Nadu downloads use GitHub even when online map viewing is off. Address lookup is separate and stays off unless configured.
 Cloud drafting is optional and off by default. It sends selected journal text to the provider you configure; presets include proprietary services and a compatible endpoint can be used. Private zones and hidden stops filter outgoing sources, but you should review the sharing preview yourself. Device speech recognition may use a network service.
 The F-Droid build contains no Google Play Services, advertising SDK or analytics SDK. It does not include the developer's managed cloud-backup configuration. Its Android location backend does not use Google's activity-transition sleep mechanism, so battery usage can differ from the Google-backed build.
 Requires Android 8 or newer. Background capture depends on permissions and device power settings. DailyBeat is not an attendance verifier, navigation system, emergency tool or evidence-custody system. Tamil Nadu offline maps provide basemaps, not offline address search or turn-by-turn navigation.

fdroid:com.freeftp.app.name: FreeFTP
fdroid:com.freeftp.app.summary: Free FTP, FTPS and SFTP client. No ads, no paid tier, no tracking.
fdroid:com.freeftp.app.description:
FreeFTP connects your phone to your own servers over FTP, FTPS and SFTP. It is
free in both senses: no advertising, no paid tier, no analytics, and no account.
The app talks to your servers and to nothing else. It holds one network
permission, and the only host it ever contacts is the one you typed in.
Features
* FTP, FTPS (explicit and implicit) and SFTP in a single client.
* Browse, download, upload, rename, delete and create folders.
* Read files without downloading them. Tap any text file and it is streamed
 straight into memory, with nothing written to your storage. The encoding is
 detected and shown, so you can tell real content from mojibake.
* Download whole folders, recursively, with their structure preserved.
* Multi-select: long-press to start, then download or delete in bulk. Large jobs
 ask for confirmation first, and deleting always asks.
* A transfer queue with live progress, pause, resume, cancel and retry. A paused
 transfer keeps what it has and continues from that point.
* Downloads land in your Downloads folder, where you can actually find them, or
 in any folder you choose. No storage permission is requested: you grant access
 to the one folder you pick.
Security
* SSH host keys are checked. An unrecognised server is refused until you have
 seen its SHA-256 fingerprint and accepted it, and a key that later changes is
 refused outright.
* TLS certificates are verified for FTPS, with an explicit opt-in for
 self-signed ones.
* Passwords, key passphrases and private keys are encrypted at rest with a key
 held in the Android key store.
* Password, SSH key (with passphrase) and anonymous authentication, falling back
 automatically across publickey, password and keyboard-interactive.
FreeFTP handles the awkward parts of real-world FTP: passive and active mode,
MLSD with a LIST fallback, a dozen server listing dialects, UTF-8 negotiation,
and resuming an interrupted transfer.

fdroid:com.shubhang.loophole.name: Loophole
fdroid:com.shubhang.loophole.summary: One-tap Quick Settings toggle for Android Developer Options.
fdroid:com.shubhang.loophole.description:
Loophole is a one-tap Quick Settings toggle for Android Developer Options.
If you're an Android developer, Developer Options is basically always on. But a lot of banking and fintech apps treat that as a red flag and refuse to open, or silently degrade, while it's enabled -- even though you're not doing anything shady, you're just building.
The normal fix is: open Settings, find Developer Options, toggle it off, open your banking app, then remember to turn it back on later. Loophole turns that into one tap from the notification shade.
Features:
* Reads and toggles Developer Options directly via a Quick Settings tile
* Optional home screen widget as an alternative to the tile
* Simple in-app switch as a fallback / status view
* No ads, no analytics, no tracking
Setup note: toggling Developer Options programmatically requires the WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS permission, which Android only allows to be granted manually once via adb (it cannot be requested through a normal runtime permission dialog):
adb shell pm grant android.permission.WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS
Full setup instructions are in the project README.
A note on permissions: the app does not make network requests and holds no INTERNET permission. However, the manifest does include ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE, WAKE_LOCK, RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED, and FOREGROUND_SERVICE. These come from Jetpack Glance, the framework used to build the home screen widget, which relies on WorkManager internally to schedule widget updates and survive process death. They are a byproduct of the widget framework itself, not of any network or background activity Loophole performs.

fdroid:eu.radio_science_institute.smart_.name: Smart Radio Telescope
fdroid:eu.radio_science_institute.smart_.summary: Control an Az/El/polarization radio telescope mount over your local WiFi
fdroid:eu.radio_science_institute.smart_.description:
Smart Radio Telescope is the mobile client for a self-built satellite-dish radio
telescope with a motorised Azimuth / Elevation / Polarization mount. It
connects over your local WiFi to the telescope's Raspberry Pi controller and
turns a phone into its control station.
SKY VIEW AND RADIO MAPS
* All-sky dome with stars, constellations and the dish's current pointing
* Radio sky overlays from the Haslam 408 MHz and HI4PI hydrogen-line surveys,
 so you can see where the sky is bright at radio wavelengths
* Object catalogue with the Sun, the Moon and radio targets such as Cas A,
 Cygnus X, W51, IC 443, M31 and 3C 273, each with a short description and
 its rise and set times
* Tap a star or object to point the dish at it
RASTER SCANS
* Drag a rectangle on the sky to map it
* Choose the sweep axis, the pattern, the speed and the number of rows
* Watch the map fill in as a live heatmap while the dish sweeps
* Share the finished scan as an image
SOURCE TRACKING
* Eight bright radio sources ready to observe: Cas A, Cyg A, Tau A, Vir A,
 Cen A, Sgr A*, Orion A and Fornax A
* Shows which of them rise high enough at your site
* One tap starts tracking; the mount follows the source across the sky
MOUNT CONTROL
* Big STOP button, homing of all axes or one at a time, wake and sleep
* Go to horizontal (Az/El/Pol) or equatorial (RA/Dec) coordinates, or track
 an RA/Dec position
* Travel-range hints and warnings before a target would hit an endstop
* Step buttons with a configurable step size
* Virtual joystick for driving azimuth and elevation by hand: the speed
 follows your finger, the dish stops the moment you let go, and a red rim
 shows when an axis has reached its travel limit
LIVE TELEMETRY
* Position, motion and homing state of each axis, pushed live from the mount
* Endstop switch levels and the motor controller's temperature
* Live radio signal chart with minimum and maximum
* A clear banner when telemetry goes stale or the mount refuses a command
SYSTEM
* Health of the Raspberry Pi: temperature, load per core, memory, disk and
 uptime, plus the firmware and backend versions
* Clean shutdown of the Pi from the app, with a confirmation step
* Works in portrait and landscape
HARDWARE COMPANION
This is a hardware companion app: it does nothing on its own. It requires the
matching open-source telescope hardware and Raspberry Pi backend, which are
part of the same project. The app talks only to a device you run yourself on
your own network — it contacts no external servers, and nothing it reads
leaves that network. For development and classroom demos, the project also
ships a simulator that stands in for the mount.
LOCATION
While the telescope's backend knows no better position than its fallback,
the app asks for the phone's location once per connection — and offers a
button to ask again — and sends it only to that backend. The backend uses
it for pointing, shows it to the telescope's other clients and writes it to
its log; it does not keep it past a restart. The app itself stores no
location. You can also enter the site by hand in the settings; a phone or
GPS position takes precedence over a hand entry.
Built as a school demonstrator for radio astronomy.

Oxu turns books, documents and web pages into calm, plain text you can read and translate.
 How it works 
 Open a file or a web page, its text appears on screen
 Long-press to select the sentence you want
 Tap "Translate" and read it in your own language
 What you get 
 PDF, EPUB, DOCX, ODT, FB2, HTML and plain text files
 Web reader: open a link, or share it from your browser, and read only the article text, without menus, ads or pictures. Pages you read stay available offline
 Text shared from any app opens straight in the reader
 Offline translation on your phone with Mozilla's Firefox Translations models: download the languages you need, nothing leaves the device
 21 languages, including English, Turkish, Azerbaijani, Russian, German, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese and Japanese. You pick both the language of the text and the language to translate into
 Adjustable text size and a dark theme, no account, no ads, no tracking
 Recent files and pages that remember where you stopped
 Three translation backends: offline (on device), MyMemory (an online service, free, no API key, daily limit) or LibreTranslate (your own server, no limits). Online services can fall back to downloaded languages when there is no connection
 Privacy 
 Oxu has no analytics. Reading works entirely offline. Network requests are
only made for what you ask for: the translation of the text you selected (sent to
the online service you chose in Settings, or nowhere with offline translation),
downloading the offline language list and models from Mozilla, and loading a web
page you opened.
 Requirements 
 Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer. Scanned or image-only PDFs contain no text to
extract, so they are not supported.

firefox-addons:2611259.name: Tab Sorter
firefox-addons:2611259.summary: Tab Sorter Extension. Organize Your Browser Tabs Efficiently. Tab Sorter is a browser extension that helps you organize your open tabs using various sorting methods. Keep your browsing organized and find tabs quickly.
firefox-addons:2611259.description:
Tab Sorter Extension
Organize Your Browser Tabs Efficiently
Tab Sorter is a browser extension that helps you organize your open tabs using various sorting methods. Keep your browsing organized and find tabs quickly.
Features
Sorting Options
- By Title - Alphabetical organization
- By URL/Domain - Group similar websites together
- By Favicon - Visual grouping by site icons
- Most Recently Used - Sort by recent activity (Firefox only)
- Shuffle - Randomize tab order
Keyboard Shortcuts
- Ctrl+Shift+Space - Sort tabs with your preferred method
- Ctrl+Shift+L - Extract domain (move same-domain tabs to new window)
Additional Features
- Auto-sort - Automatically organize new tabs
- Cross-window support - Works across all browser windows
- Bilingual interface - English and French support
- Privacy-focused - No data collection, local processing only
How to Use
 Install the extension from your browser store
 Click the Tab Sorter icon or use keyboard shortcuts
 Select your preferred sorting method
 Your tabs will be organized instantly
Browser Compatibility
 Firefox - Available on Mozilla Add-ons
 Chrome/Chromium - Available on Chrome Web Store
 Works with all Chromium-based browsers
Installation
Firefox
Visit the Firefox Add-ons Store to install.
Chrome
Visit the Chrome Web Store to install.
Privacy
 No data collection
 Local processing only
 Minimal permissions required
 Open source code
Support
For questions or issues, visit the GitHub repository: https://github.com/etienneschalk/tab-sorter-firefox/issues 
Tab Sorter - Keep your tabs organized.

firefox-addons:3071313.description:
PageWarp transforms the website you are viewing into a nostalgic retro web experience.
Choose from 1980s Synthwave, 1990s GeoCities, Early 2000s Web, MySpace, and Windows 95 styles. Customize the look with colorful themes, Light, Authentic, or Chaos intensity, retro cursors, scrolling banners, decorative stamps, custom homepage titles, and visitor numbers.
Features:
 Turn PageWarp on with one click
 Automatically enable it on every website
 Keep the mode active while navigating links
 Choose different retro web eras and themes
 Use custom cursors and optional sound effects
 Exclude specific websites
 Capture and save screenshots locally
 Always-visible PageWarp status control
PageWarp only changes webpage appearance locally. It does not collect browsing history, use analytics, require an account, upload screenshots, or send webpage data to external servers.

apple-macos:1619241039.description:
History Book automatically saves your browsing history for searching later.
By default, it only auto-saves pages that contain an article, so you don’t have to worry about it saving your sensitive data.
If you want, you can configure it to auto-save every webpage. If you are feeling paranoid, you can disable auto-save entirely. You can also exclude websites that you never want to auto-save.
You can use it as a read-it-later app, but I mostly use it as a search app.
For privacy reasons, History Book stores your browsing history in iCloud. Apart from the iCloud sync, History Book does not collect, store, or transmit any personal information.
History Book has no in-app purchases, no ads, and no tracking. It’s a universal purchase, so you only have to buy it once to use it on iPhone, iPad, and Mac.
Caveat:
- The app uses readability.js to check whether a webpage is readable. It is likely to produce both false positives and false negatives.
- The app is written in SwiftUI, which means there are some not-quite-standard behaviors and UI bugs that I can’t fix.
- The app uses iCloud for syncing.

apple-macos:6810548352.name: TravelTalk-English
apple-macos:6810548352.description:
Progress in English listening never comes from how much you consume — it comes from repeated practice within a fixed set of sentences and scenes, until you develop real sensitivity to pronunciation. That sensitivity is the foundation for everything else. 
TravelTalk deliberately offers no endless content: 33 travel scenarios, around 600 sentences. That is the entire corpus — by design. A small, fixed corpus is what makes deep repetition possible. The 20th time you hear a sentence, your ear catches what the 2nd time never could.
[The practice loop] 
 ・Listen to the model recording, with sentences chunked by real speech pauses (not punctuation guesses)
 ・Slow down to 0.83x with one tap to hear every pause between chunks 
 ・Record yourself and compare with the model, line by line 
 ・Not satisfied? Long-press to delete and record again
[Eye-care design]
 ・Both dark and light modes are tuned to reduce glare — no harsh pure white 
 ・No ads, no pop-ups, no social feeds. Your attention stays on practice 
[Privacy] 
 ・Recordings are stored only on your device 
 ・The app works fully offline: zero network requests, zero data collection 
[A note to learners] 
Before you start, we honestly recommend learning standard Cambridge/Oxford pronunciation rules first (e.g. English Pronunciation in Use). Then come back and drill every scene in this app. 
This app is a gym, not a school: it gives you the tools for deliberate practice — an ear that hears the difference, and a mouth that can fix it.
